To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the plausibility ranges for the adult HIV prevalence estimates are −18% to 19% for generalised epidemic countries, −38% to 102% for LLC countries with medium quality surveillance, −53% to 183% for LLC countries of low quality surveillance, −38% for the Eastern and Southern African region and +67% for the Western and Central Africa region.
The bounds are intended as a guide as what reasonable or plausible range are for the uncertainty of the HIV incidence, prevalence and mortality estimates.
the uncertainty in HIV prevalence estimates is greater for low-level or concentrated epidemic countries than for countries with generalized epidemics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing a method to determine the uncertainty of HIV estimates for a particular country or region.
the following questions: What is the uncertainty in the current HIV estimates?
the problem of estimating HIV prevalence and AIDS incidence in countries where HIV surveillance data are not available.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the plausibility of a country having an HIV prevalence of 1.0% is much more likely than having a prevalence of 0.1%.
the plausibility bound for the HIV prevalence estimate for the adult population in a particular country is between the lower and upper bound of the range.
the plausibility bound for a given country or region should be interpreted as a range of values that are plausible for the HIV estimates for that country or region.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the uncertainty in the estimates for generalised epidemic countries is relatively small, while for LLC countries it is relatively larger.
we are able to make a reasonable guess about the HIV epidemic in the world, but we are not able to quantify the degree of uncertainty about our guess.
plausibility bounds can help policy makers to understand the uncertainty in the estimates and the factors that contribute to the uncertainty, and to make better informed policy decisions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
countries should conduct population based HIV surveys to better understand their HIV epidemics and to improve the plausibility of the HIV estimates.
there are a number of factors which influence the uncertainty in the estimates.
there is still a need for more HIV surveillance data to be collected in countries, especially those that have not yet done so, and that the surveillance data collected should be of high quality.
